chapter_title: Yoga — A Way of Life (Sports and Wellness)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge and Reading the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.121): paired discussion on prior yoga knowledge and International Yoga Day.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange: ask students what they already know about yoga and what 21st June is known for. Take two or three responses from the class to surface existing knowledge and build curiosity.

Read the passage aloud together — teacher models, then students follow paragraph by paragraph — covering the origin of yoga, Sage Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, and the WHO mYoga app (p.121–127). Pause briefly after each sub-section to allow students to ask a clarifying question.

Invite students to list words they know related to yoga and share them across the class, building a running word-cloud on the board from their contributions. Close by asking one student to read the Sanskrit shloka from the Hatha Yoga Pradipika aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may conflate yoga purely with physical stretching; steer early responses toward the text's emphasis on the unity of mind, body, and breath. The prose_summary notes that the text traces yoga's roots to Sage Patanjali — ensure that connection is made during reading. Students unfamiliar with Sanskrit terms may need the meaning of 'yuj' (to join or to unite) pointed out explicitly.
materials: Textbook — Yoga — A Way of Life (p.121–127)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.124): fill blanks using words from the box to consolidate passage understanding.
Let us think and reflect (p.124): discuss the aim of yoga and the idea of unity.

time_bands.activity: Students work individually to complete the fill-in-the-blank paragraph from “Let us discuss” (p.124), choosing from the word box [sleep / lifestyle / health / strength / calm / stress / balance]. Teacher then invites students to read their completed sentences aloud and the class confirms or corrects each blank together.

Move to “Let us think and reflect” (p.124): pose the question about the aim of yoga and take two student responses, then open a whole-class discussion on the idea of unity — how yoga joins mind, body, thought, action, and human beings with nature as described in the passage. Guide students toward textual evidence rather than personal opinion alone.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the passage together and discussed yoga's origins, students are now connecting specific vocabulary to concepts. A common difficulty is distinguishing 'mental benefits' from 'physical benefits' — encourage students to point to the relevant paragraph when justifying their answers. The questions about the WHO mYoga app and long-term effects of yoga (from “Let us think and reflect”) are rich but time-intensive; they are available as self-study in the textbook (p.124) for students who wish to explore further.
materials: Textbook — Yoga — A Way of Life (p.124)

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Personal Account and Sharing Yoga Thoughts

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.125): select four true statements from a set of seven after listening.
Let us speak (p.126): share yoga thoughts in groups of four using sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Set the scene: tell students they will hear a girl describe her experience of practising yoga with her grandfather. Ask students to keep the seven statements in front of them (p.125) and mark as they listen.

Read the transcript aloud clearly at a measured pace (p.129). After reading, students individually select the four true statements. Discuss answers as a class, asking students to point to the part of the text that confirms or contradicts each statement.

Move into “Let us speak” (p.126): form groups of four and give students an unhurried turn to share their yoga thoughts using the provided sentence starters, covering both those who have tried yoga and those who have not. Teacher circulates, prompting hesitant speakers and encouraging active listening within groups.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript (p.129) states the grandfather began practising yoga at age 16 — not that he has practised for 16 years — a distinction several students are likely to miss; draw attention to this after the listening task. For the speaking activity, students who are reluctant to share may be invited to respond to a classmate's statement rather than initiate, reducing pressure while keeping them engaged.
materials: Textbook — Let us listen (p.125) and Let us speak (p.126)

periods.activity_title: Planning and Drafting a Paragraph on Yoga Benefits

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.127): draft a short paragraph on the benefits of yoga using sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a short paragraph structure on the board: opening sentence, two or three supporting points, and a concluding sentence — drawing examples from the passage on physical, mental, and systemic benefits. Students discuss in pairs which benefit they find most compelling before writing.

Students draft their paragraph independently (p.127), using the sentence starters provided as scaffolding. Teacher circulates, offering brief one-on-one prompts to students who are stuck on a supporting idea, and encouraging them to use vocabulary from the passage.

Pairs exchange drafts and give one piece of specific peer feedback — one thing the writer did well and one suggestion for a stronger supporting idea. Each student revises one sentence in light of the feedback before the close of the unit. Volunteers share a sentence or two with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed both physical and mental benefits during comprehension work, students can draw confidently on the passage's content here. Watch for paragraphs that list benefits without explanation — the sentence starters in the textbook model explanation ('because...'), so remind students to use them as a thinking tool, not decoration. Students who finish early may be invited to add the Sanskrit shloka's idea of asana to their paragraph.

periods.activity_title: Exploring 'Practice' and 'Practise' — Noun and Verb Pairs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.125): fill blanks correctly with practice (noun) or practise (verb) in six sentences.
Let us learn (p.125): write two sentences each using advice (noun) and advise (verb).

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'practice' and 'practise' on the board and elicits the rule: 'practice' is a noun, 'practise' is a verb. Students find one example of each in the passage (p.121–127) before the exercise begins.

Students complete the six fill-in-the-blank sentences (p.125) individually. Teacher takes answers aloud, asking students to name the grammatical role of the word (subject, object, verb) each time as justification, and corrects any errors on the board.

Introduce the parallel pair 'advice' (noun) / 'advise' (verb) from p.125. Students write two sentences each and share with a partner for peer checking, then two or three pairs share with the class. Teacher invites students to notice the pattern: the noun ends in '-ce', the verb in '-se'.

periods.teacher_notes: The passage itself uses 'practice' and 'practise' in context (p.121–127), so students can verify their understanding against a real source they have already read. Students at this level often over-generalise the '-ce'/'-se' rule — note that not all noun-verb pairs follow it, so encourage caution. The word-making activity from “Let us learn” (p.125) using the letters Y, r, e, a, n, G, o is a worthwhile self-study challenge students can explore independently.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Yoga Through the Ages and Today

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.127): research two yoga asanas, their names, and benefits; present findings to the class.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief whole-chapter recollection: invite students to name one fact about yoga's origin, one health benefit, and one thing they noticed about the English words 'practice' and 'practise' — drawing together the informational, language, and personal dimensions of the chapter. Accept a range of responses without evaluating them yet.

Students work in pairs to research two yoga asanas using information from the textbook, their own knowledge, or the UN/MyGov web references named in “Let us explore” (p.127). They note each asana's name, its physical description, and at least one benefit. Each pair prepares a spoken two-minute presentation — no written product is required; notes on a scrap of paper are sufficient.

Selected pairs present their asanas to the class. After each presentation, the teacher connects the asana's benefit back to the passage's categories — physical, mental, or systemic — reinforcing the text's framework. Close by asking students to reflect aloud: how does the chapter's idea that mind and breath must accompany every asana change how they think about exercise in general?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together yoga's ancient origins (the Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation dating to 2700 BC), its global recognition through International Yoga Day and the WHO mYoga app, and the language learning about 'practice' and 'practise' — students can connect across these strands regardless of which units they previously encountered. If students cannot access the web references in class, they can draw solely on the passage and their own experience; the task is structured to work either way. The reflection question on mind-breath-body unity is the conceptual heart of the chapter and a good closing point.

items.source_context: Yoga's origin in Sanskrit 'yuj', Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, physical and mental health benefits, WHO mYoga app launch 2021.
items.item_stem: According to the passage 'Yoga — A Way of Life', which of the following correctly describes the meaning of the Sanskrit root 'yuj' from which the word 'yoga' is derived?

options.label: A
options.text: To stretch and strengthen the body through physical postures.

options.label: B
options.text: To join or unite, symbolising harmony between mind, body, and nature.

options.label: C
options.text: To quieten the mind through silent meditation alone.

options.label: D
options.text: To follow the teachings of Sage Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this focus only on the physical dimension of yoga, missing the passage's broader definition of unity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has conflated the aim of yoga (quieting the mind, from Patanjali) with the meaning of the word 'yuj' itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates a confusion between the etymology of 'yoga' and Sage Patanjali's role as the systematiser of yoga practice.

items.item_stem: The passage states that the World Health Organisation launched the WHO mYoga app in June 2021. What does this development reveal about how the world now views the practice of yoga? Support your answer with reasoning from the passage.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The launch of the WHO mYoga app shows that yoga is now recognised globally as a valuable health practice, not just a cultural tradition of India. By making the app free and worldwide, the WHO acknowledged yoga's documented benefits for physical, mental, and systemic health.

items.source_context: A girl's account of practising yoga with her grandfather, breathing exercises in the park, grandfather's fitness at 65.
items.item_stem: Listen to the spoken account of the girl who practises yoga with her grandfather. Then read each statement below and write True or False. Give a reason for each answer.

options.text: The girl does simple yoga exercises together with her grandfather.
Her grandfather started practising yoga when he was sixteen years old.
The girl plans to learn asanas from her grandfather during the summer vacations.
Her grandfather is fit because he eats at irregular times.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the girl says she does simple yoga exercises with her grandfather.
2. True — the girl states her grandfather has been practising yoga since he was 16 years old.
3. True — she says she plans to learn asanas from him during the summer vacations.
4. False — the transcript says he eats a balanced diet regularly; irregular meals are not mentioned.

items.source_context: A girl's account of practising yoga with her grandfather, breathing exercises in the park, grandfather's fitness at 65.
items.item_stem: In the spoken account, the girl says she does breathing exercises on the morning of an Inter-House competition. What does this tell you about how she understands the purpose of yoga? Write your answer in two to three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The girl uses breathing exercises not just as physical activity but as a way to manage anxiety and improve concentration before a stressful event. This shows she understands yoga as a tool for mental calm and focus, not only for bodily fitness.

items.item_stem:
Read the two sentences below and explain why a different form of the word is needed in each. Then write your own original sentence using each form correctly.

(a) 'Daily practice of yoga, as described in the passage, improves both physical and mental health.'
(b) 'The passage seems to practise what it preaches by explaining each benefit clearly.'

For each sentence: name whether the highlighted word (practice, practise) is a noun or a verb, and write one new sentence of your own using that form in a context related to health or school.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: In sentence (a), 'practice' is a noun — it names the act of doing yoga regularly. In sentence (b), 'practise' is a verb — it describes the action the passage performs. A noun form can be replaced by 'the habit' or 'the routine'; a verb form can be replaced by 'does' or 'performs'.

items.item_stem: The passage mentions that seals from the Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation (dating to 2700 BC) suggest yoga was practised in ancient India. Using information from the textbook passage, your own research, or the UN Yoga Day resources, write a short account (eight to ten sentences) describing: (a) how yoga has changed from ancient times to the present day, and (b) one asana you found in your research — its name, what you do in it, and one benefit it offers. Include at least one fact not mentioned in the textbook passage.

expected_elements: Mentions yoga's ancient origins (Sindhu-Sarasvati or Patanjali) accurately.
Describes a present-day development such as International Yoga Day or WHO mYoga app.
Names one asana with a clear description of what the practitioner does.
States one benefit of that asana, linked to physical, mental, or systemic health.
Includes at least one fact not found in the textbook passage, showing independent research.

items.item_stem: Design a one-page informational poster titled 'Yoga — Ancient Wisdom, Global Practice'. Your poster must include: (a) a brief note on yoga's origins (ancient India, Patanjali, or the Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation), (b) two yoga asanas with their names and one benefit each, and (c) one reason why yoga is celebrated internationally today. Write the text for each section of your poster in clear, informative sentences suitable for a school display. You do not need to draw illustrations — write only the text you would put in each section.

expected_elements: Origins section accurately names an ancient source (Patanjali, Sindhu-Sarasvati, or Sanskrit 'yuj').
Two asanas named with a clear, accurate benefit each.
International relevance mentioned (International Yoga Day, WHO mYoga app, or UN recognition).
Language is clear, informative, and appropriate for a school display audience.
